question: Which song by The Beatles starts with a chord jump from the tonic to the minor fitfh chord?

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The opening that is normally quoted in the theory literature is the i – v opening of Eleanor Rigby.

The piece is in E minor. The string quartet intro is laid out

E minor – B minor – …

i = E minor is the tonic of the piece and the chord that follows it is the
minor fifth-degree chord of the key, v = B minor, the chord whose root is a
perfect fifth above the tonic. In the classic i–v lament form that is the
first two-chord jump you hear, E–B, tonic to the minor fifth-degree chord,
before the progression goes on to G major and so on. 

The same i–v tonic-to-minor-fifth opening is the one that is most often
cited for the Beatles’ minor-key instrumentals, e.g. Yer Blues / In My
Life etc., in E minor the textbook i–v is the E minor – B minor opening of
Eleanor Rigby. That is the tritone-free minor-fifth-degree jump that is
meant by a tonic → v jump.

If the jump is taken in the strict interval sense I → ♭V, a tritone/root-a-
minor-fifth jump, the classic Beatles tritone intro quoted in the literature
is the C-major → G♯/Ab major/minor colouring that opens Come Together /
I Am The Walrus, the Beatles’ best-known tonic-to-flat-five, tonic-to-minor-
fifth-interval, opening.
